title: The Eiffel Tower was only ever meant to be temporary.
description:
The Eiffel Tower was only ever meant to be temporary. Raised for the 1889 World's Fair, 300 metres of iron marking a century since the Revolution, it was an exhibit, not a monument. The city fully intended to take it down again.

That was the length of Gustave Eiffel's permit. When it ran out, the tower was to be dismantled and sold for scrap. The date set for its demolition was 1909.

Its own artists signed a protest to stop it. In 1887 Maupassant, Dumas, Gounod and others petitioned against the 'useless and monstrous' tower, a 'hateful column of bolted sheet metal' over the city. The most famous shape in Paris began as an eyesore.

To save his tower, he made it useful. He funded army wireless experiments from the top, and by 1909 a military radio station beneath it made it indispensable. Paris renewed the lease, and the demolition never came.

In the First World War, the aerial that had saved it intercepted German signals before the Battle of the Marne.

Sources:
- https://www.toureiffel.paris/en/the-monument/eiffel-tower-and-science (Official Eiffel Tower website, Societe d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel, 'The Eiffel Tower and science'; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the tower was to be destroyed 20 years after construction; that Gustave Eiffel promoted scientific uses to save it; that on 5 November 1898 Eugene Ducretet made the first wireless telegraphy contact between the tower and the Pantheon; that from 1903 Eiffel funded Captain Gustave Ferrie's military wireless experiments from the tower, whose concession was due to end in 1909; that in 1909 an underground military radiotelegraphy station was set up and the City of Paris renewed the concession on 1 January 1910; and that in the First World War the tower's station intercepted German communications before the Battle of the Marne.
- https://www.toureiffel.paris/en/the-monument/history (Official Eiffel Tower website, 'Origins and Construction of the Eiffel Tower'; read in full 27 August 2026): established that the tower was built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle marking the centenary of the French Revolution, stood 300 metres tall, and was completed on 31 March 1889; and that in 1887 a 'Protest against the Tower of Monsieur Eiffel', signed by figures including Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod, Alexandre Dumas junior and Charles Garnier, condemned the 'useless and monstrous' tower as a 'hateful column of bolted sheet metal'.
